title: Now and last weekend
cando: say what is happening now, and tell someone what you did

about.text: In this lesson you talk about now and about last weekend. You read a story and a form about a lost bag. Then you say sorry because you missed a party.
goals: Say what you are doing now: I'm making coffee.
Ask about the past: How was your weekend? What did you do?
Say what you did: I worked. We went out. We had a lot of fun.
Read a short story and a lost property form.
Leave a phone message to say why you missed a party.

chapters.title: How was your weekend?
chapters.text:
In this lesson you talk about now, and about last weekend.
First, you listen to two colleagues, Carlos and Mei. It is Monday morning, in the office kitchen.
Mei asks: What are you doing? Carlos says: I'm making coffee. That is about now.
Then Mei asks: How was your weekend? What did you do? That is about the past.
Listen to the end of the past verbs. Worked ends in a t sound. Played ends in a d sound.
Visited has one more part: vis-it-ed.

chapters.title: Now and the past
chapters.text:
For now, use am, is or are, and a verb with -ing. I'm cooking. She's working. What are you doing?
For the past, most verbs add -ed. I worked. We played football. I visited my aunt.
Some verbs change. Go is went. Have is had. See is saw.
To ask about the past, use did. Did you go out? What did you do?
After did, the verb does not change. Say: Did you go? Not: Did you went?

chapters.title: A lost bag
chapters.text:
Next, you read a short story, The green bag. Amina is late, and she leaves her bag on the bus.
Then you read a form for lost things. It says what she lost, when and where.
Then you write a message to say why you were late. Say sorry, and say what happened.

chapters.title: A phone message
chapters.text:
In the task, you missed a colleague's party. You phone her, but she doesn't answer.
So you leave a message. Say sorry, and say why.
Then she calls you back. She asks about your weekend. Tell her three things you did.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a short story about a weekend.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: It's Monday morning at work. A colleague asks: How was your weekend? What do you say?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. At work, people often ask this on Monday. A short answer is fine. Then ask back: How was yours?

conversation.title: Monday morning
conversation.setting: It is Monday morning. Carlos is in the office kitchen. His colleague Mei comes in.
lines: Morning, Carlos! What are you doing?
I'm making coffee. Do you want a cup?
Yes, please! So, how was your weekend?
It was great, thanks. I visited my brother in Leeds.
On Saturday we played football, and in the evening we went out.
To a party at his friend's flat. The music was great. We had a lot of fun.
That's nice. My weekend was boring. I worked on Saturday!
Yesterday I went to see a film. It was boring, too!
Never mind. Your holiday starts next week, right?
Yes! It's a trip to Scotland with my sister.

questions.q: Who did Carlos visit at the weekend?
questions.why: Carlos says: I visited my brother in Leeds.

questions.q: What did Mei do on Saturday?
questions.why: Mei says: I worked on Saturday!
Mei says: It's a trip to Scotland with my sister.

phrases.use: A friendly question on a Monday.
Saying you left home to have fun: a party, a film, a meal.
Saying: it's OK, it's not important.

items.meaning: The day before today.
items.example: Yesterday I worked until eight o'clock.

items.meaning: To go and see a person or a place.
items.example: I visited my parents at the weekend.

items.meaning: To use your eyes. Also: to watch a film, or to meet a person. The past is saw.
items.example: We saw a great film on Saturday.

items.meaning: To go to a café, a party or a film, to have fun. The past is went out.
items.example: We went out for dinner on Friday.

items.meaning: People meet to eat, drink, talk, dance and listen to music.
items.example: There's a party at my flat on Saturday. Can you come?

items.meaning: A story on a screen, at the cinema or on TV.
items.example: We watched a funny film last night.

items.meaning: A game for two teams. The players kick a ball.
items.example: I play football with my colleagues on Thursdays.

items.meaning: The sounds of songs. You listen to it, or you play it.
items.example: I listen to music on the train to work.

items.meaning: To do a sport or a game. Also: to make music on a guitar or a piano.
items.example: Do you play football?

items.meaning: Days with no work. You rest, or you go to a new place.
items.example: I'm on holiday next week.

items.meaning: You go to a place for a short time, and then you come back.
items.example: We went on a trip to the sea.

items.meaning: A good, happy time.
items.example: The party was great. We had a lot of fun.

items.meaning: Very, very good.
items.example: The music was great!

items.meaning: Not fun. Nothing happens, and you want it to stop.
items.example: The meeting was very boring.

sound.title: The -ed ending
sound.explain: The -ed ending has three sounds. In worked, it sounds like t. In played, it sounds like d. After t or d, it is a new part: vis-it-ed. So say work-t, not work-ed. Listen, then say each group.

sayIt.instructions: Say Carlos's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Can you hear the end of each past verb?
lines: It was great, thanks. I visited my brother in Leeds.
On Saturday we played football, and in the evening we went out.
To a party at his friend's flat. The music was great. We had a lot of fun.
Never mind. Your holiday starts next week, right?

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Two are about now. Three are about last weekend.
spot.question: Which sentences are about now? Which are about the past? How do you know?
spot.answer: Now: are you doing, I'm making. They use am, is or are, and -ing. The past: visited, went, did. Visited adds -ed. Went is the past of go. A question about the past uses did.

rules.title: Now: I'm cooking
rule: am, is, are + verb + -ing: I am cooking. She is working.
Say it short: I'm cooking. He's sleeping. We're waiting.
Ask: What are you doing? Are you working? Yes, I am.
No: I'm not working. It isn't raining.
Spelling: make – making, sit – sitting, study – studying.
rules.mistake: Not: I cooking. Not: I am cook. Say: I am cooking.

rules.title: The past: worked, went, had
rule: Most verbs add -ed: work – worked, play – played, visit – visited.
Some verbs change: go – went, have – had, see – saw.
Ask with did: Did you go out? What did you do?
Answer: Yes, I did. No, I didn't.
After did and didn't, the verb does not change: I didn't go.
rules.mistake: Not: Did you went out? Say: Did you go out?

practice.q: Tomasz can't talk now. He ___ driving.
What are you ___ ? — I'm cooking dinner.
practice.why: What are you doing? asks about now.
Last Sunday is in the past: visited.

practice.q: We ___ to the cinema last Friday.
practice.why: Go changes in the past: went.
A question about the past: Did you …?

practice.q: Did you ___ the football on TV?
practice.why: After did, the verb does not change: see.

practice.q: Last night I ___ a great time at the party.
practice.why: Have changes in the past: had.

practice.q: No, I ___ go out. I stayed at home.
practice.why: No, in the past: didn't + a verb.
Look! means now: it is raining.
Yesterday is in the past: worked.

yourTurn.prompt: A friend sends you two questions: What are you doing now? What did you do last weekend? Write two sentences for each question.
yourTurn.model: Now I'm sitting on the bus. I'm going to work. On Saturday I worked in the morning. In the evening I went out with friends. On Sunday I visited my parents.

text.title: The green bag, and a lost property form
text.body:
THE GREEN BAG
Last Friday, Amina finished work late. She ran to the bus stop, but she missed the bus.
The next bus came at half past six. Amina was very tired.
She put her green bag on the seat next to her. Her purse was in it.
At her stop, she got off quickly. She forgot her bag!
At home, she phoned the bus company and left a message.
On Saturday morning, they called her back. “We found your bag!”

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE FORM: this bus company does not exist.
NORTHWAY BUSES: LOST PROPERTY
Name: Amina Yusuf
Phone: 07700 900 146
What did you lose? A green bag with a red purse in it
When? Friday 15 May, about 6.45 pm
Where? On the number 9 bus, from King Street
Did you lose a passport or a wallet? Please tell the police too.

gist.a: A woman forgot her bag on a bus.
wrong: A bus driver lost his wallet.
gist.why: Amina got off the bus quickly, and she forgot her bag.

gist.a: telling the bus company about a lost thing
gist.why: The form says: Lost property. What did you lose?

detail.q: Why was Amina on the later bus?
detail.why: She ran to the bus stop, but she missed the bus.

detail.q: What was in the green bag?
detail.why: The story says: Her purse was in it.

detail.q: When did the bus company call Amina?
detail.why: The story says: On Saturday morning, they called her back.

detail.q: You lost your passport on a bus. What does the form say?
detail.why: The form says: Did you lose a passport or a wallet? Please tell the police too.

items.meaning: Something is not with you, and you don't know where it is. The past is lost.
items.example: I often lose my keys.

items.meaning: To see something that you looked for. The past is found.
items.example: I found my wallet under the sofa.

items.meaning: Not to remember something. The past is forgot.
items.example: Sorry, I forgot your name.

items.meaning: To be too late for a bus or a train. Also: not to go to a party or a class.
items.example: I missed the train, so I was late for work.

items.meaning: A small, flat case for money and cards. It goes in your pocket or bag.
items.example: My bank card is in my wallet.

items.meaning: A small bag for your money. You keep it in a bigger bag.
items.example: I left my purse at home, so I can't pay.

items.meaning: A small book with your photo and name. You need it to travel to other countries.
items.example: Don't forget your passport!

items.meaning: Their job is to keep people safe. You call them when something bad happens.
items.example: I lost my passport, so I told the police.

items.meaning: Words you send to a person, or leave on their phone.
items.example: I left a message for my manager.

model.title: A message: why I was late
model.body:
Hi Ana,
I'm very sorry I was late this morning.
I missed the 8:10 bus, and the next bus was 20 minutes late.
I got to work at 9:30.
I can stay late tonight and finish the report.
Sorry again!
Omar

write.task: You were late for work, a class or a meeting with a friend. Write a message to say sorry. Say why you were late. It can be real or made up.
write.starter: Hi …, I'm very sorry I was late …
checklist: I said why: I missed …, I forgot …, I lost …
I used past verbs: missed, was, got …
I wrote my name at the end.

card.title: Sorry I missed it!
card.situation: Your colleague Priya had a birthday party on Saturday. You didn't go, because you missed the train. The next train was two hours later. On Monday you phone Priya, but she doesn't answer.
card.goal: Leave a message: say sorry, and say why you missed the party. Then Priya calls you back. Tell her about your weekend.

phrases: Hi Priya, it's … . Sorry I missed your party!
I missed the train, and the next one was two hours later.
I'm really sorry. I hope it was fun.
Call me back when you can.
It was great. / It was boring.
prepare.notes: Make notes. Why did you miss the party? What did you do at the weekend? Write three things. Use past verbs: missed, went, visited, saw.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, leave your message for your teacher. Then your teacher is Priya. She calls you back and asks about your weekend.
doIt.wehel: You are my colleague Priya. I missed your birthday party on Saturday. First, read my phone message. Then call me back. Ask me about my weekend: What did you do? Where did you go? Was it fun? Use simple English.

model.title: The message and the call back
lines: Hi, this is Priya. Please leave a message.
Hi Priya, it's Omar. Sorry I missed your party! I missed the train, and the next one was two hours later. I'm really sorry. Call me back!
Hi Omar! I got your message. Don't worry!
Yes, it was great. So, what did you do at the weekend?
On Saturday I went home and watched a film. It was boring!
I visited my cousin. We played football in the park.
Nice! What are you doing now?
I'm waiting for the bus. See you at work!
compare: Did you say sorry, and say why you missed the party?
Did you ask Priya to call you back?
Did you use past verbs: missed, went, visited, played?
Did you answer What are you doing? with I'm + -ing?

canDo: I can ask and say what someone is doing now.
I can ask about the past with did.
I can say what I did at the weekend.
I can read a short story and a lost property form.
I can leave a phone message to say why I missed something.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first picture. Who are the people? What do you think they did?
reading.talk: Was the weekend in the story good or boring? What did you do last weekend? Write two or three sentences, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.why: What are you doing? asks about now.

quiz.q: We ___ football in the park last Sunday.
quiz.why: Last Sunday is in the past: played.
After did, the verb does not change: go.

quiz.q: I ___ the bus, so I was late for work.
quiz.why: You miss a bus when you are too late for it.

quiz.q: My money and bank cards are in my ___ .
quiz.why: A wallet is for money and cards.

quiz.q: The film was very ___ . Nothing happened!
quiz.why: Boring: nothing happens, and you want it to stop.

quiz.q: Which past verb has one more part, like vis-it-ed?
quiz.why: After t or d, -ed is a new part: wait-ed.

quiz.q: I've got a headache. — You ___ take a tablet and rest.
quiz.why: Should + a verb, with no to.

quiz.q: The blue jacket is £30. It's ___ than the black one.
quiz.why: A short word adds -er: cheap, cheaper than.

quiz.q: Go ___ the post office and turn right.
quiz.why: Go past: walk by it, and do not stop.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the Monday morning conversation in pairs. Then change the weekend: a trip, a party, a quiet day at home. Listen for the -ed endings.
Day 2: a mime game for now: one learner acts, and the others ask Are you cooking? Are you swimming? Then learners ask Did you…? questions about last weekend and report back.
Day 3: the task. Each learner leaves you a phone message about the missed party. Then you are Priya: call back and ask about their weekend.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and read two learners' “why I was late” messages aloud.
